title: The Structure of the Atom
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Chemistry
summary: The Rutherford model of the atom, the charges of protons, neutrons and electrons, the gold foil evidence for the nucleus, and the electrostatic attraction that holds every atom together.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Describe the Rutherford model of the atom: a tiny, positive nucleus at the centre with electrons moving around it, and mostly empty space. (8Cm.01)
Know the charges of the three particles: electrons are negative, protons are positive and neutrons have no charge. (8Cm.02)
Know that the attraction between positive and negative charges (electrostatic attraction) is what holds an atom together. (8Cm.03)

blocks.text: 2. Atoms are made of smaller particles

In Stage 7 you learned that every substance is made of particles, and that an **element** is made of only one type of **atom**. Atoms are far too small to see, even with the best light microscope — a line of about 10 million atoms would be only 1 mm long. But scientists found that atoms themselves are made of even smaller particles: **protons**, **neutrons** and **electrons**.

blocks.title: A memory trick
items: **P**roton = **P**ositive.
**N**eutron = **N**eutral (no charge).
**E**lectron = the **E**xtra-light one, on the **E**dge, negative.

blocks.text: An atom has the **same number of protons and electrons**. Each proton has one positive charge and each electron has one negative charge, so the charges cancel. This is why an atom is **neutral** — it has **no overall charge**. Neutrons have no charge, so the number of neutrons makes no difference to the overall charge.
3. The Rutherford model of the atom
The picture of the atom used today at this stage is the **Rutherford model** (also called the **nuclear model**). It has four key ideas you must be able to describe:

items: At the centre is a **tiny nucleus**. It is **positive** because it contains the protons. It also contains the neutrons.
Almost **all the mass** of the atom is in the nucleus.
The **negative electrons** move around the nucleus, a long way from it.
Most of the atom is **empty space**.

blocks.text: **How small is the nucleus?** If an atom were blown up to the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea on the centre spot, and the electrons would be like specks of dust flying around the outer seats. Everything in between is empty space. This comparison is an **analogy** — it helps you picture something you can never see.
4. How the model was discovered
Models in science change when new evidence is found. The story of the atom is a famous example.

rows: Discovered the **electron**, a tiny negative particle inside atoms. So atoms are not solid, unbreakable balls.
Suggested the **plum pudding model**: a ball of positive charge with negative electrons stuck in it, like fruit in a pudding.
Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden (working for Ernest Rutherford)
Fired positive **alpha particles** at very thin gold foil — the **gold foil experiment**.
Explained the results with a new model: a tiny positive **nucleus** with electrons around it — the **Rutherford model**.
Discovered the **neutron**, the particle with no charge in the nucleus.

blocks.text: 5. The gold foil experiment — evidence for the nucleus

Alpha particles are tiny, fast-moving particles with a **positive** charge. Geiger and Marsden fired them at a sheet of gold foil only a few hundred atoms thick, and recorded where they went. If the plum pudding model were right, the positive charge would be spread thinly everywhere, so all the alpha particles should go straight through or bend only very slightly. That is not what happened.

blocks.caption: Gold leaf, hammered so thin that it crumples like tissue paper. Gold can be beaten thinner than any other metal, so Geiger and Marsden could use a gold foil only a few hundred atoms thick.

headers: What it tells us about the atom
rows: Most of the atom is **empty space**.
There is a **positive** charge in the atom that **repels** the positive alpha particles (like charges repel).
The positive charge is packed into a **tiny** centre — the **nucleus** — which also holds **most of the mass**.

blocks.title: Exam technique — observation then conclusion
blocks.text: Checkpoint often gives you one observation and asks what it shows. Always link the two: "**Most** went straight through, **so** the atom is mostly empty space." Use the words **most / a few / very few** exactly — they carry the marks.
6. What holds an atom together?
You already know from magnets and static electricity that **opposite charges attract** and **like charges repel**. The same rule works inside atoms.

blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 500 200" width="500" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13"><circle cx="120" cy="110" r="75" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.1" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><circle cx="120" cy="110" r="14" fill="#fff4d6" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="120" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">+</text><circle cx="195" cy="110" r="10" fill="#e3f4e5" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="195" y="114.5" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">−</text><line x1="183" y1="110" x2="154.8" y2="110" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.6"/><polygon points="150,110 157.4,106.9 157.4,113.1" fill="#0f1b33"/><text x="168" y="100" text-anchor="middle">pull</text><text x="250" y="70">The positive nucleus and the</text><text x="250" y="88">negative electron attract each</text><text x="250" y="106">other (electrostatic attraction).</text><text x="250" y="134">This pull keeps the electron in</text><text x="250" y="152">the atom, moving around the</text><text x="250" y="170">nucleus instead of flying away.</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Electrostatic attraction between the positive nucleus and a negative electron.

items: The nucleus is **positive** (it contains protons). The electrons are **negative**.
Opposite charges attract, so every electron is pulled towards the nucleus. This pull is called **electrostatic attraction**.
Electrostatic attraction is what **holds the atom together**: it keeps the electrons in the atom, moving around the nucleus, instead of flying away.
Neutrons have no charge, so they are **not** attracted to the electrons. (A different, very strong force holds the protons and neutrons together inside the nucleus — you will meet it in later years.)

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية
blocks.text: الذرة فيها نواة صغيرة جدًا في المنتصف، موجبة الشحنة لأن فيها البروتونات (+)، ومعاها النيوترونات (بدون شحنة). الإلكترونات (−) بتلف حوالين النواة، ومعظم الذرة فراغ. الموجب والسالب بيتجاذبوا — ده اسمه التجاذب الكهروستاتيكي — وهو اللي بيمسك الإلكترونات في الذرة. عدد البروتونات = عدد الإلكترونات، علشان كده الذرة متعادلة (مالهاش شحنة).
7. Models and analogies

Nobody has ever seen a proton or an electron directly, so scientists use **models**. An **analogy** is a kind of model that compares the atom with something familiar. Every analogy has strengths and weaknesses — Checkpoint can ask for both.

headers: How it is like the atom
How it is not like the atom
rows: **The Solar System**: Sun in the middle, planets moving around it
Small centre with most of the mass; things moving around it; mostly empty space
Planets are held by gravity, electrons by electrostatic attraction; planets are not charged; the Sun is not made of protons and neutrons
Shows how tiny the nucleus is compared with the whole atom
A stadium has a solid floor and seats; an atom is mostly empty space
**Plum pudding**: fruit stuck in a cake
Was a useful model of the old (Thomson) idea
Wrong for real atoms: the positive charge is not spread out, it is in a tiny nucleus

blocks.text: 8. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Complete the table about the particles in an atom. [3]

items: Row 1: proton → **positive (+)**.
Row 2: the particle with no charge is the **neutron**; it is found in the **nucleus**.
Row 3: electron → **negative (−)**, **moving around the nucleus** (outside the nucleus).
Marking: usually 1 mark per correct row. **Common mistake:** writing "neutral" for the electron, or putting electrons inside the nucleus.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — An atom of boron has 5 protons and 6 neutrons. (a) How many electrons does it have? [1] (b) How many particles are in the nucleus? [1] (c) Explain why the atom has no overall charge. [1]

items: (a) Atoms are neutral, so electrons = protons = **5**.
(b) Nucleus = protons + neutrons = 5 + 6 = **11** particles.
(c) The 5 positive charges of the protons are cancelled by the 5 negative charges of the electrons; neutrons have no charge.
**Common mistake:** in (a), giving 6 (the number of neutrons) — the electron number always matches the **proton** number in an atom.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — In the gold foil experiment, **a few** alpha particles were deflected. Alpha particles are positive. What does this tell you about the atom? [2]

items: There is a **positive charge** inside the atom (1)…
…which **repels** the positive alpha particles, because like charges repel (1).
**Common mistake:** "they hit electrons". Electrons are far too light to push an alpha particle off course — it was the positive nucleus.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — Explain what holds the electrons in an atom. Use ideas about charge in your answer. [2]

items: The nucleus is positive (it contains protons) and the electrons are negative (1).
Opposite charges attract, so there is an **electrostatic attraction** that pulls the electrons towards the nucleus and keeps them in the atom (1).
**Exam tip:** name **both** charges and use the word **attract/attraction**. "Gravity" or "the neutrons hold them" scores 0.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — A teacher says: "If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be the size of a pea in the middle." (a) What does this analogy show about the nucleus? [1] (b) Give one way in which the analogy is **not** like a real atom. [1]

items: (a) The nucleus is **very small compared with the whole atom** (the atom is mostly empty space).
(b) Any one: a stadium is full of solid seats and air, but an atom is mostly empty space / a pea has no charge but the nucleus is positive / the pea does not hold most of the mass of the stadium.
**Exam tip:** a question about an analogy wants a comparison with the real thing — always mention the **real** atom in your answer.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — An atom has 8 protons, 8 neutrons and 8 electrons. It gains 2 extra electrons. Is it still neutral? Explain. [2]

items: It now has 10 negative electrons but only 8 positive protons — there are **2 more negative charges**, so its overall charge is **negative (−2)** (1).
(A charged particle like this is called an **ion**. You will study ions in later years; at Stage 8 you just need to count the charges.)

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying the **nucleus** has no charge. The nucleus is **positive** — it contains protons. The **neutron** is the particle with no charge.
Putting electrons **inside** the nucleus. Only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.
Thinking the number of neutrons changes the overall charge. Neutrons have no charge.
Saying "the atom is solid". The Rutherford model says the atom is **mostly empty space**.
Mixing up observation and conclusion in the gold foil experiment — "most went straight through" is what was **seen**; "mostly empty space" is what it **shows**.
Writing "gravity" or "magnetism" for what holds the atom together. The answer is **electrostatic attraction** between opposite charges.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Label a diagram** of an atom: nucleus, proton, neutron, electron.
**Complete a table** of particles, their charges and where they are found.
**Count** protons, neutrons and electrons from a diagram, then state the overall charge.
**Describe** the Rutherford model (2–3 marks): tiny positive nucleus, most of the mass, electrons around it, mostly empty space.
**Gold foil**: "What does this observation show?" — link most / a few / very few to empty space / positive charge / tiny dense nucleus.
**Explain** what holds the atom together — positive nucleus, negative electrons, opposite charges attract.
**Evaluate an analogy**: one way it is a good model and one way it is not.

blocks.title: احفظ الجدول ده
items: البروتون (proton): موجب +، في النواة.
النيوترون (neutron): بدون شحنة، في النواة.
الإلكترون (electron): سالب −، بيلف حوالين النواة، وكتلته صغيرة جدًا.
في تجربة رقائق الذهب: معظم الجسيمات عدّت ← الذرة معظمها فراغ. قليل انحرف ← النواة موجبة. نادر جدًا ارتد ← النواة صغيرة جدًا وفيها معظم الكتلة.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: The structure of the atom — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: Which particle in an atom has **no** charge?
questions.e: Neutrons have no charge (they are neutral). Protons are positive and electrons are negative. The nucleus is not a single particle — it contains protons and neutrons, so it is positive overall.

questions.q: Name the tiny central part of an atom where the protons and neutrons are found.
questions.e: The **nucleus** is the tiny, positive centre of the atom. It holds the protons and neutrons and almost all of the atom's mass.

questions.q: (d) What is the overall charge of this atom?
c: no overall charge, because there are 4 protons and 4 electrons
positive, because the nucleus is positive
negative, because electrons move around the outside
positive, because there are more neutrons than electrons
questions.e: 4 positive charges (protons) cancel 4 negative charges (electrons), so the atom is **neutral**. Neutrons have no charge, so the number of neutrons does not change the overall charge.

questions.q: In the gold foil experiment, **most** of the alpha particles went straight through the gold foil. What does this show about atoms?
c: Atoms are solid balls with no gaps.
questions.e: If most alpha particles passed through without hitting anything, most of the atom must be **empty space**. The experiment did not show neutrons (they were found later, in 1932).

questions.q: In the gold foil experiment a very small number of alpha particles bounced back towards the source. Alpha particles are positive. Explain what this showed about the centre of the atom. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: the centre/nucleus is positive (so it repelled the positive alpha particles / like charges repel). 1 mark: the nucleus is very small (only very few particles hit it) AND/OR contains most of the mass / is dense. Accept 'massive' or 'heavy' for the second mark. Do not accept 'the electrons pushed them back'.
questions.e: Only a positive charge could repel (push back) the positive alpha particles, so the centre of the atom must be **positive**. Because only very few particles bounced back, the positive centre must be **tiny**; and because it could turn a fast alpha particle right round, it must hold **most of the mass** of the atom. This tiny, dense, positive centre is the nucleus.

questions.q:
Write the missing word to complete the sentence.
The negative electrons are held in an atom by electrostatic ________ to the positive nucleus.
questions.e: Opposite charges **attract**. The pull between the positive nucleus and the negative electrons is called **electrostatic attraction**, and it holds each atom together.

questions.q: An atom of sodium has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. How many electrons does it have?
questions.e: An atom has no overall charge, so the number of electrons = the number of protons = **11**. The 12 neutrons have no charge, so they do not affect this.

questions.q: An atom of iron has 26 electrons and 30 neutrons. How many particles are in its nucleus altogether?
questions.e: Step 1: the atom is neutral, so protons = electrons = 26. Step 2: the nucleus holds protons and neutrons: 26 + 30 = **56** particles. Common mistake: adding the electrons too (26 + 26 + 30 = 82) — electrons are **outside** the nucleus.

questions.q: An atom of lithium has 3 protons and 3 electrons. It **loses** one electron. What is the overall charge now?
c: it depends on the number of neutrons
questions.e: Now there are 3 positive charges (protons) and only 2 negative charges (electrons). There is one more positive than negative, so the particle is **positive** (+1). Neutrons have no charge, so they never change the overall charge.

questions.q:
A student says: "An atom is like the Solar System."
Give **one** way the analogy is a good model of the atom, and **one** way it is not a good model. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark for a strength, e.g. the Sun is at the centre like the nucleus / the planets move around the Sun like electrons move around the nucleus / most of the Solar System is empty space, like the atom / most of the mass is in the centre (the Sun), like the nucleus. 1 mark for a weakness, e.g. planets are held by gravity but electrons are held by electrostatic attraction / the Sun is not made of smaller particles like protons and neutrons / planets are not charged / each planet has its own path but several electrons can share the same path / planets are all different sizes but all electrons are the same.
questions.e: **Good:** the Sun is in the centre and the planets move around it, just as the nucleus is at the centre and electrons move around it; both are mostly empty space with most of the mass at the centre. **Not good:** planets are held by gravity, but electrons are held by **electrostatic attraction** between opposite charges; and the Sun is not made of protons and neutrons.

questions.q: Describe **two** differences between the "plum pudding" model of the atom and the Rutherford model. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark each, up to 2: plum pudding has the positive charge spread through the whole atom / Rutherford has the positive charge in a tiny nucleus at the centre; plum pudding has electrons stuck inside the positive ball / Rutherford has electrons moving around the nucleus; plum pudding atom is solid / Rutherford atom is mostly empty space; Rutherford model has most of the mass in the nucleus. Each difference must say what both models show (or clearly compare).
questions.e: (1) In the plum pudding model the positive charge is spread through the whole atom; in the Rutherford model all the positive charge is in a **tiny nucleus** at the centre. (2) In the plum pudding model the electrons are stuck inside the positive 'dough'; in the Rutherford model the electrons **move around the nucleus** and the atom is **mostly empty space**.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Proton: positive, in the nucleus. Neutron: no charge, in the nucleus. Electron: negative, moves around the nucleus.
Rutherford model: tiny positive nucleus with almost all the mass, electrons around it, mostly empty space.
Gold foil: most straight through → empty space; a few deflected → positive centre; very few bounced back → tiny, dense nucleus.
Atoms are neutral: number of protons = number of electrons.
Electrostatic attraction between the positive nucleus and the negative electrons holds the atom together.
